title: Seven Towers, One Harbor
sum: After the deaths of the seven brothers (chapters 8-12), the speaker draws the lesson: godly reason is master of the passions. Had the brothers eaten the defiling food, passion would have won; instead they turned back from nothing, not even fire. Their reasoning was like seven towers at a harbor's mouth that keep the water calm inside. He recalls how they cheered one another: let us die like brothers, copy the three young men in the furnace, remember Isaac, give our souls back to God who gave them, and fear the one who can torment the soul forever, not the man who thinks he can kill us. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will receive us.

Then the speaker turns to what made their courage hardest: they loved one another. He describes brotherly love almost like a natural scientist, from the womb they shared to the milk they drank and the law they learned together. That love grew stronger with godliness, yet the brothers who were left watched the others die and held out.
readings: Read as a philosophical proof

The chapter is the conclusion of a demonstration. The speaker states the thesis (13:1), sets out the case that would disprove it (13:2), and shows it did not happen (13:3-5). Then he raises the hardest objection: love between brothers. If even that passion was mastered, the case is closed. The brothers do not stop loving each other; reason rules their love (3:5).
Read as a martyr story

The brothers' words to each other (13:9-18) are a short liturgy of martyrdom: a call to die together, models from Scripture (the three in the furnace, Isaac), a vow to give back the soul to God, a warning against fear, and the promise of a welcome from the patriarchs. Christian martyr stories later used the same pieces.

views.H: Historians note that this chapter adds to 2 Maccabees 7, which has no group speech of the brothers and no description of their love for one another. The speaker builds the scene for his argument. Townshend (1913) saw in such rhetoric a writer at home in Greek learning, addressing Jews who knew it too.
views.N: Readers of the New Testament hear echoes: do not fear those who kill only the body (Matthew 10:28; 13:14-15), welcome by the patriarchs after death (Luke 16:22; 13:17), and brotherly love (philadelphia, Romans 12:10). These show a shared Jewish language about martyrdom and the afterlife; the chapter does not prove that any New Testament writer read this book.
views.G: The chapter is close to Stoic language, "master in its own right" and "good reasoning", but its view of the passions is not Stoic. For the Stoics the wise man feels no passions at all; here the brothers keep their love for one another, and reason rules it (compare 3:2-5). Natural love is a gift of "God's providence" (13:19), not a fault to be uprooted.

deep.h: Love that reason does not kill
deep.b:
The speaker could have praised the brothers for feeling nothing. He does the opposite. He spends nine verses (13:19-27) on how strong their love for one another was: they shared a womb, were shaped over the same months, grew from the same blood, drank the same milk, and were trained in the same law. Their love was not weakened by godliness but made "even more precious" by it (13:26). The point is that the brothers who were left "watched their brothers being abused and tortured to death" and still held out (13:27), and even urged them on (14:1).

This is where the book parts from strict Stoicism, which taught that the virtuous person is free of passions. Here reason is not the uprooter of the passions but their opponent (3:5). The brothers win not by ceasing to love, but by loving God and his law more. In this the book is closer to the Bible's own picture, where love of family is commanded (Exodus 20:12) and still gives way when God asks for more (Genesis 22; Luke 14:26).

echoes: Daniel 3:1-30; Genesis 22:1-19; Matthew 10:28; Luke 12:4-5; Luke 16:22; Matthew 8:11; Romans 12:1; Romans 12:10; Hebrews 11:34; 2 Maccabees 7:1-42; 1 Maccabees 2:59

title: The Mother Who Loved More
sum: The speaker breaks into praise: the brothers' reasoning was more royal than a king's and freer than free men, a holy harmony of seven. None of them was a coward; they ran toward death as if on the road to immortality, moving together like the limbs of one body, circling the number seven like the days of creation. We shudder just to hear of it; they lived through it, in fire.

Then he turns to the greatest proof: their mother. A woman's mind, he says, mastered pains more varied than her sons'. He shows how strong a parent's love is from nature: tame birds shield their chicks, wild birds circle crying around their nests, even bees fight to the death for their hive. Yet love for her children did not move this mother, whose soul was like Abraham's.
readings: Read as rhetoric

The chapter has two movements: a hymn of praise to the brothers (14:2-10) and an argument from nature (14:11-20). The examples from animals were standard in Greek moral speech; the speaker uses them to make the mother's love as large as possible before he shows her mastering it.
Read with Genesis 22

The last verse holds the key to the chapters that follow: the mother had a soul "like Abraham's" (14:20). As Abraham was ready to give up Isaac, she gives up seven sons. The comparison runs through 15:28, 16:20, 17:6 and 18:20.

views.H: The praise of the mother (14:11-17:6) goes far beyond 2 Maccabees, which praises her in a few verses (2 Maccabees 7:20-23). Townshend (1913) noted the speaker's openness to Greek images and thought it suited a Jewish writer in a Greek city.
views.J: Jewish tradition remembered the mother of seven sons in many forms. Townshend (1913) reports that the medieval Hebrew history called Yosippon retells the martyrdoms much as 4 Maccabees has them and names the mother Hannah. He judged that the book's direct influence on Jewish literature was otherwise not great.
views.G: The arguments from animal behavior (14:14-19) are the kind found in Greek writers on nature and ethics, who used animals to show what is "natural". The speaker's aim is to show that a mother's love is natural and good: what reason masters is not wickedness but a strong, good passion.
views.N: The race to immortality (14:5) is the same picture as Hebrews 12:1 and 2 Timothy 4:7. Jesus' picture of a mother bird gathering her young (Matthew 23:37) uses the same kind of image as 14:15-17, for God's love rather than a mother's.

deep.b:
The speaker spends six verses on birds and bees (14:14-19). His point is that a mother's love is not a weakness peculiar to women but part of nature, shared with "animals without reason". Birds that live on roofs defend their chicks; birds that nest on cliffs drive off intruders; when they cannot, they circle crying (14:17). Even bees will die for their hive. The more natural and strong this love is, the more remarkable it is that the mother could master it.

Townshend (1913) reports that Gregory of Nazianzus, preaching on the Maccabees in the fourth century, took over the picture of the mother bird and applied it directly to this mother. The law of Moses shows care for a mother bird too (Deuteronomy 22:6-7), and Jesus used one for his own love (Matthew 23:37).

echoes: Genesis 1:1-2:3; Genesis 22:1-19; Hebrews 12:1-2; 2 Timothy 4:7; Deuteronomy 22:6-7; Matthew 23:37; Luke 15:20; 2 Maccabees 7:20-23

title: Two Votes in a Mother's Soul
sum: The mother had a choice between godliness and seven sons kept safe for a short time, and she chose godliness, which keeps people safe for eternal life. The speaker explains how strong a mother's love is: mothers feel more for their children than fathers, and this mother, after seven pregnancies, loved most of all, and her sons' goodness made her love them more. Yet she urged them one by one to die. She watched their flesh melt and their fingers twitch on the ground, and she did not cry.

He addresses her directly: the only woman who gave birth to complete godliness, tested by pains worse than labor. In the council chamber of her soul she held two votes, death or safety, and she voted with Abraham. He crowns her with titles: mother of the nation, defender of the law, shield of godliness, prize-winner. Like Noah's ark in the flood, she rode out the storms against godliness.
readings: Read as a praise speech

Greek speakers knew the encomium, a formal speech of praise. Chapters 15-17 are an encomium of the mother: her nature, her love, her trial, her choice, her titles. The speaker addresses her as if she were present ("O mother"), which brings the hearers into her presence.
Read as a picture of faith

The center of the chapter is a decision (15:25-28). The mother weighs everything that pulls her to save her sons, and she chooses what lasts. She "remembered" Abraham's steadfastness (15:28): her faith is a memory of how God's people have acted before.

views.O: The Orthodox churches keep the mother among the saints on 1 August, with her seven sons and Eleazar; the Orthodox Church in America's life of the saints names her Solomonia. Townshend (1913) reports that Gregory of Nazianzus, preaching on the Maccabees, saw in her agony a foreshadowing of the Mother of God at the cross.
views.H: Scholars see the chapter as the speaker's own composition: 2 Maccabees gives the mother two short speeches and a few lines of praise (2 Maccabees 7:20-29). The detailed tortures of 15:15-20 go beyond 2 Maccabees 7 as well.
views.G: The scene of the council of the soul (15:25-26) uses the Greek picture of the soul as a city with a ruling part. The "bull-like" stare of 15:19 is the word Plato uses of Socrates as he took the poison (Phaedo 117b). The list of the sons' virtues (15:10) draws on the four virtues of Greek ethics.
views.W: Catholic and Protestant Bibles do not include 4 Maccabees: it is not in the Vulgate, the Latin Bible of the Western church, as Townshend noted (1913). Western readers have known this mother mainly from 2 Maccabees 7, which Catholic Bibles include.

deep.b:
The titles of 15:29 make the mother more than a private heroine. She is "mother of the nation", the one through whom Israel's faithfulness is born again, as Sarah was a mother of nations (Genesis 17:16). She is the law's "defender", the one who wins its case. She is a "prize-winner" in a contest fought inside her ("the contest of the heart"). And she is one who "endured more bravely than men" (15:30).

The speaker's view of women is that of his time: he assumes women are weaker and so feel more (15:5). That is the reason he gives for her greatness. But in the end he makes her the strongest proof of his whole thesis (16:1-2), stronger than Eleazar and stronger than her sons. 2 Maccabees had already called her "good beyond all measure" (2 Maccabees 7:20).

title: The Lament She Did Not Make
sum: The speaker states his case as proved: if even an old woman, the mother of seven, could watch her sons tortured to death, godly reason is sovereign over the passions. Daniel's lions and the furnace of Mishael were less fierce than the love that burned in her, yet she put it out. He imagines what she would have said if she had been weak: seven pregnancies for nothing, no grandchildren, no son to bury her. She said none of it. She urged her sons on, as though she were giving birth to them again, into immortality.

Then he tells what she did say. Arrested with her sons, she watched Eleazar tortured and spoke to them in Hebrew: the contest is noble; it would be shameful for you to fear what an old man has endured; you owe your life to God; remember Abraham, who did not cower from sacrificing Isaac, and Daniel, and Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael. With these words she persuaded them to die rather than break God's commandment, because they saw that those who die for God live to God.
readings: Read as a speech within a speech

The chapter holds two speeches: one she did not give (16:6-11) and one she did (16:16-23). The first gives full voice to a mother's grief, then sets it aside. The second shows what godly reason sounds like: memory of Scripture, duty to God, shame at cowardice, and hope.
Read with 2 Maccabees 7

In 2 Maccabees the mother encourages her sons with the hope of resurrection: the Creator "will give you back the breath and the life in his mercy" (2 Maccabees 7:23). Here her hope is that they "live to God" (16:25) and that she bears them again "into immortality" (16:13). The same scene carries a different hope.

views.H: The speech of 16:16-23 is set during Eleazar's torture, which joins two stories that 2 Maccabees keeps apart (2 Maccabees 6:18-31; 7). Historians see the speaker shaping the story around his argument. The list of heroes (16:20-21) is like the one in 1 Maccabees 2:51-60.
views.N: "Those who die for God's sake live to God" (16:25) is close to Jesus' answer about the patriarchs: "to him all are alive" (Luke 20:38). The roll call of Abraham, Daniel and the three is like Hebrews 11:17-19 and 11:33-34. The calling to a "contest" for the "testimony" of the nation (16:16) is language the church later used for its own martyrs.
views.J: The binding of Isaac (16:20) became a central story in Jewish thought about martyrdom; here Abraham is the model for a mother who offers her sons. Townshend (1913) reports that Yosippon, a medieval Hebrew history, gives the mother a long speech to her youngest son and calls her Hannah.
views.O: Townshend (1913) reports that the Byzantine commentator Nicetas defended Gregory of Nazianzus's view that the Maccabees were true martyrs before Christ, against some who said they died only for the law and abstinence from pork.

deep.b:
Verse 13 is the hinge of the book's hope. The mother is "bearing the full number of her sons again, this time into immortality". She gave birth to them once into the world; now, by urging them to die, she gives birth to them into deathless life. The image turns the most painful moment of a mother's life into a second labor.

The hope is different from 2 Maccabees. There, the mother says that the Creator "will give you back the breath and the life in his mercy" (2 Maccabees 7:23) and she hopes to "receive you back with your brothers" (2 Maccabees 7:29): a resurrection of the body. 4 Maccabees retells the same mother without that hope and speaks instead of immortality (16:13), living to God (16:25), standing beside God's throne (17:18) and "souls that are pure and immortal" (18:23). The New Testament holds both a life with God after death (Philippians 1:23) and a resurrection of the body (1 Corinthians 15:42-44); see the chapter 18 page.

title: A Contest of God, a Life in Exchange
sum: The guards reported that when the mother was about to be seized, she threw herself onto the fire so no one would touch her. The speaker praises her: with her sons she broke the tyrant's force, stood like a roof on pillars in an earthquake, and now shines in heaven with her star-like sons. He imagines an epitaph on their tomb: here lie an old priest, an old woman and seven sons, killed by a tyrant who wanted to destroy the Hebrews' way of life; they won justice for their nation, fixing their eyes on God.

Then he pictures their deaths as a divine contest. Virtue judged it, the prize was incorruption, Eleazar fought first, then the mother and the brothers; the tyrant was their opponent and the world looked on. The fear of God won and crowned her athletes. Now they stand beside God's throne. Because of them the enemy did not overcome the nation, the tyrant was punished and the land was cleansed: they became, as it were, a life in exchange for the nation's sin, and through their blood and their atoning death divine providence saved Israel. Even Antiochus held up their endurance as an example to his soldiers.
readings: Read as athletic contest

Verses 11-16 are a full picture of the Greek games: judge, prize, contestants, opponent, spectators, crown. Greek-speaking Jews knew the games in their cities; the speaker turns martyrdom into the noblest contest of all. Christians took the picture over: Townshend (1913) notes that John Chrysostom, preaching on the Maccabees, compared their struggle to athletic contests as this book does.
Read as sacrifice

One view. Verses 20-22 change the picture from games to the temple. The martyrs were "made holy", their blood and death were "atoning", and the homeland was "made clean". Many readers take these as words for sacrifice and purification: the deaths are an offering through which God turned from anger to saving Israel. Jarvis J. Williams, as the publisher's description of his book puts it, argues that 4 Maccabees presents the martyrs' deaths "as atoning sacrifices and as a saving event for Israel".
Read as a Greek votive offering

Another view. Daniel Bailey, reading Sinaiticus's noun hilasterion in 17:22, argues that the image is "essentially Greek": "the propitiatory offering of their death", a lasting gift dedicated to a god, like those victors set up after the games. He calls the rendering "their death as an atoning sacrifice" misleading, because the word "does not denote the act of sacrifice, nor are the martyrs compared with victims of sacrifice" such as those of the Day of Atonement.

views.O: The Orthodox churches honor Eleazar, the mother and her sons as saints on 1 August. Townshend (1913) reports that Gregory of Nazianzus pictured the mother running to the pyre "as to her bride-bed" and taught that the Maccabees were true martyrs before Christ. How the churches understand the martyrs' sufferings beside Christ's death is set out on the card at 2 Maccabees 7:37-38.
views.H: Historians see verses 20-22 as the book's own interpretation of the persecution's end: no other source says Antiochus held up the martyrs as an example (17:23), and Townshend (1913) doubted it. The book compresses the war of Judas into a result of the martyrs' deaths (18:4). The atonement language develops a seed in 2 Maccabees 7:37-38.
views.J: In Jewish thought the deaths of the righteous could be seen as atoning for Israel, as the martyrs' deaths are here; Sirach already says of Phinehas that "he made atonement for Israel" (Sirach 45:23).
views.N: Scholars debate how far these verses stand behind the New Testament's language about Jesus' death: the word hilasterion (17:22; Romans 3:25), a life given for others (Mark 10:45), blood that saves (Romans 5:9), the athletes and the crown (1 Corinthians 9:25; Hebrews 12:1-2). See the deep section below.
views.G: The contest of 17:11-16 uses the vocabulary of the Greek games exactly: the athlothetes (judge and prize-giver), the agon (contest), athletes, crown and spectators. Daniel Bailey argues that the noun hilasterion in Sinaiticus's text of 17:22 is also Greek: a votive offering dedicated to a god, not the lid of the ark.
views.W: Western churches, Catholic and Protestant, do not read 4 Maccabees as Scripture; it is not in the Vulgate (Townshend, 1913). Whether the sufferings of faithful people can help atone for others, beside Christ's single offering (Hebrews 10:14; Colossians 1:24), is answered church by church, with sources, on the card at 2 Maccabees 7:37-38.

deep.b:
Three words carry the passage. The martyrs became antipsychon, "a life in exchange" for the nation's sin. Through their blood and their hilasterios ("atoning") death, divine providence saved Israel. And the homeland was katharisthenai, "made clean". Eleazar asked for the same thing in his dying prayer (see 6:28-29, with the words "cleansing" and "a life in exchange"). The speaker says "as it were" (hosper): he knows he is speaking in a picture.

The idea behind it is that the persecution was punishment for Israel's sin. In 2 Maccabees the brothers say so: "We suffer for our own sins" (2 Maccabees 7:32), and the youngest asks God "to stop the anger of the Almighty" in himself and his brothers (2 Maccabees 7:38). Right after, "the Lord's anger had now turned to mercy" (2 Maccabees 8:5). 4 Maccabees makes the link explicit: the martyrs' deaths were the price, and God's saving help followed (17:20-21; 18:4).

deep.h: Its roots in the Hebrew Bible
deep.b: The pattern of one who suffers for others is in Isaiah's Servant: "He bore the sin of many, and he will step in for the rebels" (Isaiah 53:12). Phinehas "turned my rage back from the Israelites" (Numbers 25:11), and Sirach says "he made atonement for Israel" (Sirach 45:23). The law teaches that "It is the blood that makes atonement, by means of the life in it" (Leviticus 17:11). 4 Maccabees joins these threads: the blood of faithful people, given for God's law, turns God's anger and makes the land clean.

Romans 3:25. Paul says God put Christ forward as a hilasterion, "the place of atonement". In Sinaiticus 17:22 has the same noun (see the variant). Scholars disagree on whether the two belong together. Jarvis J. Williams, according to the publisher's description of his 2010 book, argues that Paul's conception of Jesus' death "both as an atoning sacrifice and as a saving event for Jews and Gentiles was significantly influenced by Maccabean Martyr Theology". Daniel Bailey argues against "paralleling Romans and 4 Maccabees": in Romans the word means the atonement lid of the ark, known from the Greek Old Testament; in 4 Maccabees it means a Greek votive offering.

Mark 10:45. Jesus came "to give his life as a ransom in place of many". The idea of a life given for many is close to antipsychon, but the words differ (lytron anti pollon). Hebrews 11:35-12:2. The tortured heroes who refused release most likely recall the martyrs as 2 Maccabees tells them; "fixing their eyes" (17:10) and the race (14:5) share Hebrews' Greek. None of these links proves that a New Testament writer read 4 Maccabees; the dates proposed for the book vary (Townshend, 1913, put it between 63 BC and AD 38; see the book's opening pages), so it may be older or younger than some New Testament books.

Christians have read 17:20-22 in two ways. Many see it as a witness to what Jews before and around the time of Jesus believed: that a righteous death could atone for others. On this reading the passage helps explain how the first Christians could speak of Jesus' death as atoning. At the same time, the New Testament claims something the book does not: that Christ's single death atones once for all: "With one offering he has made perfect, for all time, the people who are being made holy" (Hebrews 10:14). Whether the sufferings of other faithful people can share in atoning for others is a real disagreement among churches, set out on the card at 2 Maccabees 7:37-38.

Swete's apparatus records that a later hand in Codex Alexandrinus drew lines under words in 17:9 ("priest" and "aged woman"), under 17:18 and under 17:20-22, marking them out; at 17:18 and 17:20-22 Swete puts a question mark beside the hand.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the contest turned into a sacrifice on purpose
deep.b: The speaker moves straight from the athletic contest (17:11-16) to the language of sacrifice (17:20-22), with the quotation of Deuteronomy 33:3 between them (17:19). My suggestion is that the quotation is the hinge: the Greek word hegiasmenoi, "made holy", lets him turn crowned athletes into consecrated offerings. A Greek audience would know the winner's crown; a Jewish audience would know the consecrated sacrifice; one word joins them. This is my own reading of the passage's structure. Bailey's argument that hilasterion in Sinaiticus is a Greek votive gift fits it well, since victors in the games set up dedications to the gods.

settings.when: near the end of the speech
settings.why: To show that the martyrs' deaths were not defeat but victory in a contest judged by God, and that their death had saving power for Israel. The hearers are to see themselves as heirs of a nation saved through faithful death.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews of the Diaspora, the scattered Jewish communities of the Greek cities, who knew Greek schooling, theater and games and kept the law of Moses among neighbors who did not. The speech names no place or date. Townshend (1913) argued that it was addressed to Jews in Alexandria some time between 63 BC and AD 38, before the persecution of the Alexandrian Jews in AD 38-39; other places and dates have been proposed (see the book's opening pages). For readers living under Roman rule, the passage held out the hope that faithfulness under pressure was never wasted.
views: Some read the speech as given at a commemoration of the martyrs, which would explain the epitaph and the praise; the speech itself says only that it praises them "at this season" (1:10, in Greek kata touton ton kairon).

Townshend (1913) thought it more likely a lecture than a synagogue sermon, since it has no Bible text as its starting point, while noting that the evidence for synagogue practice is too thin for certainty.

title: The Mother's Last Words and the Gathering Home
sum: The speaker turns to his hearers: children of Abraham, obey this law and be godly in every way, knowing that godly reason is master of every passion. The martyrs were admired and given a share from God; through them the nation had peace and the law was restored; Antiochus was punished on earth and is punished still. Unable to break Jerusalem, he marched off against the Persians.

Then comes a surprise: a second speech of the mother to her sons. She was a pure virgin who never left her father's house; no seducer and no deceiving snake ruined her; she stayed with her husband, who died blessed when the sons were grown, after teaching them the law and the prophets: Abel, Isaac, Joseph, Phinehas, the three in the fire, Daniel, and the words of Isaiah, David, Solomon, Ezekiel and Moses. The speech ends with a cry over the bitter day of the tortures, divine Justice pursuing the tyrant, and the sons and their mother gathered in the place of their fathers, with pure and immortal souls from God.
readings: Read as the end of a demonstration
18:1-2 is the formal conclusion: the thesis is proved, and the hearers are told what to do: obey the law. Some commentators thought the speech once ended here (see below).
Read as a finale

18:6-24 brings the mother back for a last word, then gives a final picture of the tortures and the reward. Townshend (1913) argued that this "Hebraic finale", a roll call of Scripture's heroes in the mother's mouth, is the speaker's deliberate climax.

views.H: The place of 18:6-19 is debated (see below). The roll of heroes and quotations (18:11-19) is a Jewish form, like Sirach 44-50, 1 Maccabees 2:51-60 and Hebrews 11. The note that Antiochus marched against the Persians (18:6) agrees with 1 Maccabees 3:31 that he went east, though the book makes it a retreat.
views.N: The chapter's hope is life with God right after death (18:23), close to Revelation's souls before the throne (Revelation 6:9-11; 7:15). The New Testament also holds the resurrection of the body (1 Corinthians 15), which this book never mentions; the quotation of Ezekiel 37:3 (18:17) is its only hint of it.
views.J: The father's teaching from "the law and the prophets" (18:10) and the mother's memory of it show the ideal of a Jewish home that keeps Deuteronomy 6:7. The list of the righteous who suffered, from Abel to Daniel, belongs to the same tradition as the lists in Sirach 44-50 and 1 Maccabees 2:51-60.
views.G: "Pure and immortal souls" (18:23) is the language of Greek philosophy, close to Plato's teaching on the soul's immortality. Townshend (1913) thought the words imply that souls exist before the body, as the Wisdom of Solomon may say (Wisdom of Solomon 8:19-20).
views.O: The Orthodox churches honor the mother and her sons as saints whose souls are with God, and keep their memory on 1 August. Whether the soul is immortal by nature or by God's gift, and what the dead know before the resurrection, are asked on the cards at Wisdom of Solomon 3 and Revelation 6.
views.W: Western churches do not count the book as Scripture. Readers note that its teaching on the soul is close to later Christian teaching on life with God after death, while it is silent on the resurrection, which 2 Maccabees 7 and the creeds confess.

deep.h: 18:6-19: where does the mother's second speech belong?
deep.b:
The speech seems to end twice. In 18:1-2 the speaker draws his conclusion and appeals to his hearers. Then he tells of Antiochus's punishment and departure (18:3-6a), and only then, abruptly, does the mother speak again (18:6b-19), before a last picture of the tortures (18:20-21) and the reward (18:22-24). Her speech is also different: it is about her girlhood and marriage and the family's Bible lessons, not about reason and passion.

All the witnesses have it. Swete's apparatus gives readings of Alexandrinus, Sinaiticus and Venetus throughout 18:6-19, so the passage stands in all three. Swete notes that much of 18:5-24 has nearly faded in Alexandrinus. Brenton's English places the opening words of the speech in 18:7.

The case for a later addition or a misplaced passage. Townshend (1913) reports that certain commentators thought the book first ended at 18:2, chiefly because the mother's account of her early life is a digression. Other features fit that case: the speech's "these children" (18:9) has nothing to point back to, and its quotation of Ezekiel's dry bones (18:17) is the only hint of resurrection in a book that speaks only of immortal souls.

The case for the passage. Townshend argued that the ending at 18:2 would be a letdown after the epitaph and the contest, and that the speaker deliberately saved this praise of a woman's home virtues and the roll call of heroes to relieve the tension of the tortures and close in a "Hebraic" way. The speaker had already promised, at 12:7, to tell the mother's words a little later. Others argue, the same article notes, that the book's ending would be weak without these verses. The question remains open; the Plain English Translation prints the passage where the manuscripts have it.

4 Maccabees never speaks of the resurrection of the body. Its hope is the soul's life with God at death: the brothers run "on the road to immortality" (14:5); the mother bears her sons again "into immortality" (16:13); the prize is "incorruption" (17:12); they "now stand beside God's throne" (17:18); they are gathered "in the place of their fathers" with "souls that are pure and immortal" (18:23). The book also teaches eternal torment for the wicked (9:9; 12:12; 13:15), and says that the tyrant is still punished after his death (18:5).

This differs from 2 Maccabees, which tells the same martyrdoms with a clear hope of bodily resurrection: "the King of the world will raise us" (2 Maccabees 7:9). It is closer to the Wisdom of Solomon: "the souls of the righteous are in God's hand" (Wisdom of Solomon 3:1). The word "immortal" in 18:23 is a correction in two codices (see the variant), but the teaching does not depend on it. Christians hold both a life with Christ after death and the resurrection of the body (Philippians 1:23; 1 Corinthians 15:42-44). Whether the soul is immortal by nature is asked on the card at Wisdom of Solomon 3; what the dead know before the resurrection, at Revelation 6 and 2 Corinthians 5.

deep.h: The Bible in a mother's memory
deep.b: The mother's list (18:11-19) is a small Bible: law, prophets and writings. From the law: Abel and Cain (Genesis 4), the offering of Isaac (Genesis 22), Joseph in prison (Genesis 39), Phinehas (Numbers 25), and the Song of Moses, "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). From the prophets and writings: the three in the fire and Daniel (Daniel 3; 6), Isaiah's promise for those who walk through fire (Isaiah 43:2), David's words on the many troubles of the righteous (Psalm 34:19), Solomon's tree of life (Proverbs 3:18), Ezekiel's dry bones (Ezekiel 37:3). Several quotations follow the Greek Old Testament and some differ from it (see the notes). Almost every name is a righteous sufferer or a story of God giving life in death. The list ends with Moses' words from Deuteronomy 30:20: "This is your life."

settings.when: the speech gives no moment; it reads as words spoken to them before or during their trial
settings.why: To set before her sons her own purity and loyalty, their father's faith, and the stories and promises of Scripture he taught them, so that they would see their death within the long story of God's righteous sufferers and his power to give life.

views: Townshend (1913) argued that the speaker placed it here on purpose, as a relief from the tortures and a Hebraic finale.
A later addition or a misplaced passage
Some commentators, Townshend reports, held that the book first ended at 18:2; Townshend himself saw no reason to look for another hand.
